reasons: Opinion confirms: 'RECOMMENDED FOR PUBLICATION', File Name 23a0206p.06, 'UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE SIXTH CIRCUIT', 'Nos. 22-5593/5800', 'Decided and Filed: September 1, 2023', Moore, C.J.

Lake citations[] empty / slip_only true (no F.4th page locatable) — slip-op citation 'No. 22-5593, slip op. (6th Cir. 2023)' is the correct no-fabrication rendering (lead docket of the consolidated 22-5593/5800).

Consent-scope limit supported: court found consent covered only the on-site preview, not the later seizure/forensic exam ('Lewis's consent did not authorize the seizure and forensic examination of his devices').

Bare-bones affidavit / no probable cause: affidavit recited only 'During [the] search it became apparent that Mr. Lewis had used his laptop to view images...'; 'That conclusory statement was too vague and insubstantial to establish probable cause... therefore violated the Fourth Amendment's probable-cause requirement.'

Good faith unavailable: 'the good-faith exception is inapplicable here. A search-warrant affidavit that states only the affiant's conclusory belief... is a bare-bones affidavit that... precludes application of the good-faith exception.'

Opinion contains a substantive scope-of-consent holding (Section II.B.1): applying Jimeno's objective-reasonableness standard, the court affirmed that consent to a device preview did not extend to seizure/forensic exam.
'Key' placement on 'Consent Searches' is supported by that dedicated consent analysis; disclosed evidence does not contradict it.
residual_risks: The reversal's lead ground was the bare-bones-affidavit / good-faith holding; consent-scope was an alternative warrant-exception ground. The 'Key' consent home is still legitimate but the case is multi-doctrine.
